relationship_to_restored_text: Interpretive contemplative layer aligned by verse. This does not replace the source-audited restored translation.

verses.mystical_translation: The ark enters its tent amid animal offerings and communal peace-making.
David blesses the people after completing the rites.
Every woman and man receives bread and festival food; worship reaches the body.
Levites are appointed to remembrance, gratitude, and praise.
Named musicians form an ensemble around the ark.
Trumpets sound continually before the covenant symbol.
David entrusts a thanksgiving song to Asaph's community.
Gratitude becomes public testimony among peoples.
Song and speech carry memory of wonder.
Those who seek the holy name are invited into joy.
Seeking is continuous rather than possessed once for all.
Memory holds wonders and judgments together.
Israel and Jacob are addressed as servant and chosen community.
Divine judgment is imagined across the whole earth.
Covenant memory stretches beyond one generation.
Abraham and Isaac stand inside the remembered promise.
Jacob and Israel receive it as enduring commitment.
Land is spoken as inheritance, a promise that must never erase existing neighbors.
The ancestors were few and vulnerable sojourners, not an empire.
They moved among nations and kingdoms as migrants.
Powerful rulers were restrained from harming the vulnerable travelers.
Anointed status protects vulnerable people here; it does not shield powerful abusers.
The whole earth is summoned into daily announcement of rescue.
Nations are audiences and participants, not disposable enemies.
YHWH is praised above every sacred claim.
Ancient polemic contrasts human-made gods with the maker of heavens.
Splendor, strength, and joy gather before Divine presence.
Every family of peoples is invited to bring honor.
Offering and embodied reverence answer the holy name.
The earth trembles while the world is imagined as held steady.
Heaven, earth, and nations rejoice in Divine reign rather than human empire.
Sea and field become worshippers with their own fullness.
Forest trees sing before judgment that includes the earth itself.
Gratitude rests in enduring covenant-love.
A scattered people asks to be gathered and rescued without hating the nations among whom they live.
The people answer blessing with Amen and praise.
Daily worship becomes Asaph's ongoing work.
Obed-edom's large household and Hosah guard access.
Zadok's priestly community continues worship at Gibeon.
Morning and evening offerings maintain the old ritual rhythm.
Heman, Jeduthun, and named companions sustain thanksgiving.
Music and gatekeeping share the work of sacred continuity.
The assembly returns home, and David returns to a household whose unresolved voices remain outside the Chronicler's frame.

contemplative_note: The chapter's most grounded holiness is bread given to every woman and man. Its widest holiness is a creation choir of sea, field, and forest. Its most dangerous phrase—'touch not my anointed'—protects vulnerable travelers, not powerful leaders from accountability. Worship becomes truthful when it feeds bodies, honors workers, welcomes nations, and remembers the voices left outside the royal song.
